what_its_for: Ranibizumab-nuna is used to treat certain eye conditions that involve abnormal blood vessel growth or leaking in the eye. These conditions include wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), a type of vision problem caused by blood vessel leakage under the retina in people with diabetes (diabetic macular edema), and swelling of the retina caused by blocked blood vessels (retinal vein occlusion). This medicine helps slow vision loss and may even improve your vision by blocking a protein that causes these unwanted blood vessels to grow and leak.
how_to_take: Ranibizumab-nuna is NOT a medicine you take by mouth or apply yourself at home. It is given as an injection directly into your eye by a trained eye doctor (ophthalmologist) in a clinical setting. Your doctor will numb your eye before the injection so you feel as little discomfort as possible. The area around your eye will be cleaned carefully to help prevent infection. Each injection only takes a few seconds. You should NOT try to give this injection yourself.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose and how often you need injections based on your specific eye condition. In most cases, injections are given once a month, especially at the start of treatment. After your condition stabilizes, your doctor may space out your injections to every 2 to 3 months. Always keep all of your scheduled eye appointments, even if your vision seems to be improving.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your injection appointment, contact your eye doctor as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Do not skip treatments without talking to your doctor first. Missing doses can allow your eye condition to worsen and may lead to further vision loss. Try to stay on the schedule your doctor recommends.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is stored and prepared by your doctor or healthcare provider. If for any reason you are given the medicine to bring to an appointment, keep it in its original carton, protected from light, and refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Do not shake the vial. Keep it out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: After your injection, avoid rubbing or touching your eye, as this can cause infection or injury. Avoid swimming, using hot tubs, or exposing your eye to water for at least 24 to 48 hours after the injection unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid wearing eye makeup on the day of your injection. Do not drive immediately after your appointment if your vision is blurry, as the numbing drops and the injection can temporarily affect your eyesight. Wait until your vision is clear before driving.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your eye doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of the following after your injection: sudden vision changes or worsening vision, increased eye pain or significant discomfort, increased redness in or around the eye, sensitivity to light, seeing more floaters than usual, or any discharge from the eye. These could be signs of a serious eye infection (endophthalmitis) or other complications. Also call your doctor if you experience signs of a stroke or heart attack such as sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the body, sudden confusion, trouble speaking, chest pain, or shortness of breath, as these events have rarely been reported with this type of medicine.
when_it_works: Some patients begin to notice improvement in their vision within the first few months of treatment, but results vary from person to person. For many people, the main goal of this medicine is to stop further vision loss rather than fully restore lost vision. Your doctor will regularly monitor your eye health and vision to see how well the treatment is working. It is important to continue all scheduled appointments even if you feel your vision is stable.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and over): This medicine is commonly used in older adults and is generally safe for this age group. No dose adjustment is needed based on age alone. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not known if this medicine can harm an unborn baby or pass into breast milk, so your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits carefully. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustment is typically needed, but always inform your doctor of any other health conditions you have. Children: This medicine is not typically used in children.
